{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: /Users/liana/Documents/prog/buidl-guidl/ethskills-evals/artifacts/testing-quiz-003/2026-07-27T080750Z-claude-with-skill-1/workspace/.claude/skills/testing\n\n# Smart Contract Testing\n\n## What You Probably Got Wrong\n\n**You test getters and trivial functions.** Testing that `name()` returns the name is worthless. Test edge cases, failure modes, and economic invariants — the things that lose money when they break.\n\n**You don't fuzz.** `forge test` finds the bugs you thought of. Fuzzing finds the ones you didn't. If your contract does math, fuzz it. If it handles user input, fuzz it. If it moves value, definitely fuzz it.\n\n**You don't fork-test.** If your contract calls Uniswap, Aave, or any external protocol (verified addresses: `addresses/SKILL.md`), test against their real deployed contracts on a fork. Mocking them hides integration bugs that only appear with real state.\n\n**You write tests that mirror the implementation.** Testing that `deposit(100)` sets `balance[user] = 100` is tautological — you're testing that Solidity assignments work. Test properties: \"after deposit and withdraw, user gets their tokens back.\" Test invariants: \"total deposits always equals contract balance.\"\n\n**You skip invariant testing for stateful protocols.** If your contract has multiple interacting functions that change state over time (vaults, AMMs, lending), you need invariant tests. Unit tests check one path; invariant tests check that properties hold across thousands of random sequences.\n\n---\n\n## Unit Testing with Foundry\n\n### Test File Structure\n\n```solidity\n// test/MyContract.t.sol\n// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT\npragma solidity ^0.8.20;\n\nimport {Test, console} from \"forge-std/Test.sol\";\nimport {MyToken} from \"../src/MyToken.sol\";\n\ncontract MyTokenTest is Test {\n    MyToken public token;\n    address public alice = makeAddr(\"alice\");\n    address public bob = makeAddr(\"bob\");\n\n    function setUp() public {\n        token = new MyToken(\"Test\", \"TST\", 1_000_000e18);\n        // Give alice some tokens for testing\n        token.transfer(alice, 10_000e18);\n    }\n\n    function test_TransferUpdatesBalances() public {\n        vm.prank(alice);\n        token.transfer(bob, 1_000e18);\n\n        assertEq(token.balanceOf(alice), 9_000e18);\n        assertEq(token.balanceOf(bob), 1_000e18);\n    }\n\n    function test_TransferEmitsEvent() public {\n        vm.expectEmit(true, true, false, true);\n        emit Transfer(alice, bob, 500e18);\n\n        vm.prank(alice);\n        token.transfer(bob, 500e18);\n    }\n\n    function test_RevertWhen_TransferExceedsBalance() public {\n        vm.prank(alice);\n        vm.expectRevert();\n        token.transfer(bob, 999_999e18); // More than alice has\n    }\n\n    function test_RevertWhen_TransferToZeroAddress() public {\n        vm.prank(alice);\n        vm.expectRevert();\n        token.transfer(address(0), 100e18);\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Assertion Patterns\n\n```solidity\n// Equality\nassertEq(actual, expected);\nassertEq(actual, expected, \"descriptive error message\");\n\n// Comparisons\nassertGt(a, b);   // a > b\nassertGe(a, b);   // a >= b\nassertLt(a, b);   // a < b\nassertLe(a, b);   // a <= b\n\n// Approximate equality (for math with rounding)\nassertApproxEqAbs(actual, expected, maxDelta);\nassertApproxEqRel(actual, expected, maxPercentDelta); // in WAD (1e18 = 100%)\n\n// Revert expectations\nvm.expectRevert();                           // Any revert\nvm.expectRevert(\"Insufficient balance\");     // Specific message\nvm.expectRevert(MyContract.CustomError.selector); // Custom error\n\n// Event expectations\nvm.expectEmit(true, true, false, true);      // (topic1, topic2, topic3, data)\nemit MyEvent(expectedArg1, expectedArg2);\n```\n\n### What to Actually Test\n\n```solidity\n// ✅ TEST: Edge cases that lose money\nfunction test_TransferZeroAmount() public { /* ... */ }\nfunction test_TransferEntireBalance() public { /* ... */ }\nfunction test_TransferToSelf() public { /* ... */ }\nfunction test_ApproveOverwrite() public { /* ... */ }\nfunction test_TransferFromWithExactAllowance() public { /* ... */ }\n\n// ✅ TEST: Access control\nfunction test_RevertWhen_NonOwnerCallsAdminFunction() public { /* ... */ }\nfunction test_OwnerCanPause() public { /* ... */ }\n\n// ✅ TEST: Failure modes\nfunction test_RevertWhen_DepositZero() public { /* ... */ }\nfunction test_RevertWhen_WithdrawMoreThanDeposited() public { /* ... */ }\nfunction test_RevertWhen_ContractPaused() public { /* ... */ }\n\n// ❌ DON'T TEST: OpenZeppelin internals\n// function test_NameReturnsName() — they already tested this\n// function test_SymbolReturnsSymbol() — waste of time\n// function test_DecimalsReturns18() — it does, trust it\n```\n\n---\n\n## Fuzz Testing\n\nFoundry automatically fuzzes any test function with parameters. Instead of testing one value, it tests hundreds of random values.\n\n### Basic Fuzz Test\n\n```solidity\n// Foundry calls this with random amounts\nfunction testFuzz_DepositWithdrawRoundtrip(uint256 amount) public {\n    // Bound input to valid range\n    amount = bound(amount, 1, token.balanceOf(alice));\n\n    uint256 balanceBefore = token.balanceOf(alice);\n\n    vm.startPrank(alice);\n    token.approve(address(vault), amount);\n    vault.deposit(amount, alice);\n    vault.withdraw(vault.balanceOf(alice), alice, alice);\n    vm.stopPrank();\n\n    // Property: user gets back what they deposited (minus any fees)\n    assertGe(token.balanceOf(alice), balanceBefore - 1); // Allow 1 wei rounding\n}\n```\n\n### Bounding Inputs\n\n```solidity\n// bound() is preferred over vm.assume() — bound reshapes, assume discards\nfunction testFuzz_Fee(uint256 amount, uint256 feeBps) public {\n    amount = bound(amount, 1e6, 1e30);       // Reasonable token amounts\n    feeBps = bound(feeBps, 1, 10_000);       // 0.01% to 100%\n\n    uint256 fee = (amount * feeBps) / 10_000;\n    uint256 afterFee = amount - fee;\n\n    // Property: fee + remainder always equals original\n    assertEq(fee + afterFee, amount);\n}\n\n// vm.assume() discards inputs — use sparingly\nfunction testFuzz_Division(uint256 a, uint256 b) public {\n    vm.assume(b > 0); // Skip zero (would revert)\n    // ...\n}\n```\n\n### Run with More Iterations\n\n```bash\n# Default: 256 runs\nforge test\n\n# More thorough: 10,000 runs\nforge test --fuzz-runs 10000\n\n# Set in foundry.toml for CI\n# [fuzz]\n# runs = 1000\n```\n\n---\n\n## Fork Testing\n\nTest your contract against real deployed protocols on a mainnet fork. This catches integration bugs that mocks can't.\n\n### Basic Fork Test\n\n```solidity\ncontract SwapTest is Test {\n    // Real mainnet addresses — full verified list: addresses/SKILL.md\n    address constant UNISWAP_ROUTER = 0x68b3465833fb72A70ecDF485E0e4C7bD8665Fc45;\n    address constant WETH = 0xC02aaA39b223FE8D0A0e5C4F27eAD9083C756Cc2;\n    address constant USDC = 0xA0b86991c6218b36c1d19D4a2e9Eb0cE3606eB48;\n\n    function setUp() public {\n        // Fork mainnet at a specific block for reproducibility\n        vm.createSelectFork(\"mainnet\", 19_000_000);\n    }\n\n    function test_SwapETHForUSDC() public {\n        address user = makeAddr(\"user\");\n        vm.deal(user, 1 ether);\n\n        vm.startPrank(user);\n\n        // Build swap path\n        ISwapRouter.ExactInputSingleParams memory params = ISwapRouter\n            .ExactInputSingleParams({\n                tokenIn: WETH,\n                tokenOut: USDC,\n                fee: 3000,\n                recipient: user,\n                amountIn: 0.1 ether,\n                amountOutMinimum: 0, // In production, NEVER set to 0\n                sqrtPriceLimitX96: 0\n            });\n\n        // Execute swap\n        uint256 amountOut = ISwapRouter(UNISWAP_ROUTER).exactInputSingle{value: 0.1 ether}(params);\n\n        vm.stopPrank();\n\n        // Verify we got USDC back\n        assertGt(amountOut, 0, \"Should receive USDC\");\n        assertGt(IERC20(USDC).balanceOf(user), 0);\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### When to Fork-Test\n\n- **Always:** Any contract that calls an external protocol (Uniswap, Aave, Chainlink)\n- **Always:** Any contract that handles tokens with quirks (USDT, fee-on-transfer, rebasing)\n- **Always:** Any contract that reads oracle prices\n- **Never:** Pure logic contracts with no external calls — use unit tests\n\n### Running Fork Tests\n\n```bash\n# Fork from RPC URL\nforge test --fork-url https://eth-mainnet.g.alchemy.com/v2/YOUR_KEY\n\n# Fork at specific block (reproducible)\nforge test --fork-url https://eth-mainnet.g.alchemy.com/v2/YOUR_KEY --fork-block-number 19000000\n\n# Set in foundry.toml to avoid CLI flags\n# [rpc_endpoints]\n# mainnet = \"${MAINNET_RPC_URL}\"\n```\n\n---\n\n## Invariant Testing\n\nInvariant tests verify that properties hold across thousands of random function call sequences. Essential for stateful protocols.\n\n### What Are Invariants?\n\nInvariants are properties that must ALWAYS be true, no matter what sequence of actions users take:\n\n- \"Total supply equals sum of all balances\" (ERC-20)\n- \"Total deposits equals total shares times share price\" (vault)\n- \"x * y >= k after every swap\" (AMM)\n- \"User can always withdraw what they deposited\" (escrow)\n\n### Basic Invariant Test\n\n```solidity\ncontract VaultInvariantTest is Test {\n    MyVault public vault;\n    IERC20 public token;\n    VaultHandler public handler;\n\n    function setUp() public {\n        token = new MockERC20(\"Test\", \"TST\", 18);\n        vault = new MyVault(token);\n        handler = new VaultHandler(vault, token);\n\n        // Tell Foundry which contract to call randomly\n        targetContract(address(handler));\n    }\n\n    // This runs after every random sequence\n    function invariant_TotalAssetsMatchesBalance() public view {\n        assertEq(\n            vault.totalAssets(),\n            token.balanceOf(address(vault)),\n            \"Total assets must equal actual balance\"\n        );\n    }\n\n    function invariant_SharePriceNeverZero() public view {\n        if (vault.totalSupply() > 0) {\n            assertGt(vault.convertToAssets(1e18), 0, \"Share price must never be zero\");\n        }\n    }\n}\n\n// Handler: guided random actions\ncontract VaultHandler is Test {\n    MyVault public vault;\n    IERC20 public token;\n\n    constructor(MyVault _vault, IERC20 _token) {\n        vault = _vault;\n        token = _token;\n    }\n\n    function deposit(uint256 amount) public {\n        amount = bound(amount, 1, 1e24);\n        deal(address(token), msg.sender, amount);\n\n        vm.startPrank(msg.sender);\n        token.approve(address(vault), amount);\n        vault.deposit(amount, msg.sender);\n        vm.stopPrank();\n    }\n\n    function withdraw(uint256 shares) public {\n        uint256 maxShares = vault.balanceOf(msg.sender);\n        if (maxShares == 0) return;\n        shares = bound(shares, 1, maxShares);\n\n        vm.prank(msg.sender);\n        vault.redeem(shares, msg.sender, msg.sender);\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Running Invariant Tests\n\n```bash\n# Default depth (15 calls per sequence, 256 sequences)\nforge test\n\n# Deeper exploration\nforge test --fuzz-runs 1000\n\n# Configure in foundry.toml\n# [invariant]\n# runs = 512\n# depth = 50\n```\n\n---\n\n## What NOT to Test\n\n- **OpenZeppelin internals.** Don't test that `ERC20.transfer` works. It's been audited by dozens of firms and used by thousands of contracts. Test YOUR logic on top of it.\n- **Solidity language features.** Don't test that `require` reverts or that `mapping` stores values. The compiler works.\n- **Every getter.** If `name()` returns the name you passed to the constructor, that's not a test — it's a tautology.\n- **Happy path only.** The happy path probably works. Test the unhappy paths: what happens with zero? Max uint? Unauthorized callers? Reentrancy?\n\n**Focus your testing effort on:** Custom business logic, mathematical operations, integration points with external protocols, access control boundaries, and economic edge cases.\n\n---\n\n## Pre-Deploy Test Checklist\n\n- [ ] All custom logic has unit tests with edge cases\n- [ ] Zero amounts, max uint, empty arrays, self-transfers tested\n- [ ] Access control verified — unauthorized calls revert\n- [ ] Fuzz tests on all mathematical operations (minimum 1000 runs)\n- [ ] Fork tests for every external protocol integration\n- [ ] Invariant tests for stateful protocols (vaults, AMMs, lending)\n- [ ] Events verified with `expectEmit`\n- [ ] Gas snapshots taken with `forge snapshot` to catch regressions\n- [ ] Static analysis with `slither .` — no high/medium findings unaddressed\n- [ ] All tests pass: `forge test -vvv`\n"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"05c6e27b-2c33-45a9-a422-91623bbf885f","uuid":"e78db610-5d43-42f9-92be-9eaedcecb480","timestamp":"2026-07-27T08:08:39.243Z","isSynthetic":true}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5","id":"msg_011CdSDmPQHctajcCGG6EjEt","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_01XUbZMzpTcGbmt2SKAWafY8","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/Users/liana/Documents/prog/buidl-guidl/ethskills-evals/artifacts/testing-quiz-003/2026-07-27T080750Z-claude-with-skill-1/workspace/answer.md","content":"# Why the vault reverts on mainnet USDT but never against the mock\n\n## TL;DR\n\n`usdt.approve(...)` on line 2 is a **raw `IERC20` call**, not a SafeERC20 call. Real USDT's\n`approve` returns **nothing**. Solidity's generated decoder for a `bool` return sees\n`returndatasize() == 0` and executes `revert(0, 0)` — a revert with empty data, hence no reason\nstring. The mock is a stock OpenZeppelin ERC20, whose `approve` returns `true`, so the decoder is\nalways satisfied. `using SafeERC20 for IERC20` protected line 1 and did nothing for line 2, because\nSafeERC20 is opt-in **per call site, by function name** — it is not a mode you switch on for a type.\n\nFixes: `forceApprove` instead of `approve` (plus balance-delta accounting), and a fork test against\nthe real USDT + real Aave Pool as a release gate.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Why it reverts against the real deployed USDT\n\nTether's `TetherToken` (0xdAC1…1ec7, Solidity 0.4.17) predates the finalized ERC-20 ABI. Its\nmutating functions are declared with **no return value**:\n\n```solidity\n// as deployed on mainnet\nfunction transfer(address _to, uint _value) public onlyPayloadSize(2 * 32);\nfunction transferFrom(address _from, address _to, uint _value) public onlyPayloadSize(3 * 32);\nfunction approve(address _spender, uint _value) public onlyPayloadSize(2 * 32);\n```\n\nYour contract calls it through OpenZeppelin's `IERC20`, which declares `approve` as\n`returns (bool)`. For any external call with a declared return type, Solidity ≥0.8 emits roughly:\n\n```\nsuccess := call(gas(), token, 0, in, insize, 0, 0)\nif iszero(success) { returndatacopy(0, 0, returndatasize()) revert(0, returndatasize()) }\nif iszero(gt(returndatasize(), 31)) { revert(0, 0) }      // <-- fires here\nreturndatacopy(...)                                        // decode the bool\n```\n\nSequence of events on mainnet:\n\n1. The `CALL` to USDT **succeeds**. The allowance is actually written inside USDT's frame.\n2. USDT's function ends with no `RETURN` payload → `returndatasize() == 0`.\n3. Your frame hits the ABI-decoder length check, `revert(0, 0)`, and the whole transaction —\n   including the allowance write and the earlier `safeTransferFrom` — is rolled back.\n\n`revert(0, 0)` produces **zero bytes of revert data**: no `Error(string)`, no custom error selector,\nno `Panic(uint256)` code. That is exactly the \"revert carries no reason string\" you observed.\n\n### The empty revert data is itself the diagnostic\n\nIt rules out the other two lines:\n\n- **Line 1 (`safeTransferFrom`)** would revert with `SafeERC20FailedOperation(address)` (OZ 5.x) or\n  `\"SafeERC20: low-level call failed\"` (OZ 4.x) — never empty. It didn't revert anyway.\n- **Line 3 (`aavePool.supply`)** — Aave V3's `IPool.supply` is declared with no return value, so it\n  has no decode step to fail. Its own failures (`RESERVE_FROZEN`, `SUPPLY_CAP_EXCEEDED`,\n  `INVALID_AMOUNT`) surface as `Errors.*` reason strings like `\"28\"`. Also never empty.\n\nEmpty returndata on a call to a pre-ABI token is a fingerprint. Confirm it in one command:\n\n```bash\n# declared WITH a bool return -> cast fails to decode\ncast call 0xdAC17F958D2ee523a2206206994597C13D831ec7 \\\n  \"approve(address,uint256)(bool)\" 0x87870Bca3F3fD6335C3F4ce8392D69350B4fA4E2 1000000 \\\n  --from <any-holder> --rpc-url $MAINNET_RPC\n\n# declared WITHOUT a return -> succeeds, prints \"0x\" (returndatasize == 0)\ncast call 0xdAC17F958D2ee523a2206206994597C13D831ec7 \\\n  \"approve(address,uint256)\" 0x87870Bca3F3fD6335C3F4ce8392D69350B4fA4E2 1000000 \\\n  --from <any-holder> --rpc-url $MAINNET_RPC\n\ncast interface 0xdAC17F958D2ee523a2206206994597C13D831ec7   # shows the real, return-less ABI\n```\n\n### The second landmine on the same line\n\nUSDT's `approve` also carries the anti-race guard:\n\n```solidity\nrequire(!((_value != 0) && (allowed[msg.sender][_spender] != 0)));\n```\n\nYou cannot move a **non-zero** allowance directly to another **non-zero** value; you must zero it\nfirst. In *this exact* sequence it's dormant — `Pool.supply` pulls the full `amount`, so the\nallowance returns to 0 before the next deposit. It goes live the moment approved ≠ pulled: an\ninfinite approval, a partial fill, dust left by a fee-on-transfer token, or a future integration that\napproves and then takes a different branch. Being 0.4.17, that `require` has no message either — so\nwhen it does fire, it also reverts with **no reason string**. Worth closing now, for free, with the\nsame fix.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Why `using SafeERC20 for IERC20` did not protect the failing line\n\n`using L for T` **attaches** library functions as members of `T`. It never **replaces** an existing\nmember of `T`, and it cannot rename anything.\n\n- `IERC20` already has a member called `approve`. `usdt.approve(...)` resolves to that interface\n  function — a plain, unwrapped external call. There is no ambiguity for the compiler to flag.\n- SafeERC20 does not define a function named `approve` at all. It defines `safeTransfer`,\n  `safeTransferFrom`, `forceApprove`, `safeIncreaseAllowance`, `safeDecreaseAllowance` (and, in OZ\n  4.x, the deprecated `safeApprove`). Different names ⇒ nothing to shadow.\n\nSo line 1 opted in by typing `safeTransferFrom`; line 2 opted out by typing `approve`. SafeERC20's\nprotection is in `_callOptionalReturn`, which tolerates a missing return value:\n\n```solidity\n// OpenZeppelin 5.x\nfunction _callOptionalReturn(IERC20 token, bytes memory data) private {\n    bytes memory returndata = address(token).functionCall(data);\n    if (returndata.length != 0 && !abi.decode(returndata, (bool))) {\n        revert SafeERC20FailedOperation(address(token));\n    }\n}\n```\n\n`returndata.length != 0 &&` is the entire fix: zero-length returndata is treated as success, and the\naddress-has-code check lives in `functionCall`. Line 2 never reached this code.\n\n**Generalize it:** `using SafeERC20 for IERC20` is not a safety property of the contract. It is\nautocomplete. The only thing that makes a token call safe is the *name you typed at the call site*.\nA single `.approve(`, `.transfer(`, or `.transferFrom(` anywhere in the codebase is unprotected,\nand the compiler will never say so. This is why the rule has to be mechanically enforced (§4).\n\n---\n\n## 3. Why the mock could never fail, and why more mock tests would not have helped\n\n### The mock cannot disagree with you\n\n`MockERC20` is a stock OZ `ERC20`. Its `approve` ends with `return true` — 32 bytes, `0x…01`. The\ndecoder check `returndatasize() > 31` passes. There is no input, no ordering, no amount, no caller,\nand no state that makes a compliant token return zero bytes. **The failure mode does not exist in\nthe mock's state space.** The suite has been green since the first commit not because the code is\ncorrect but because the mock and the contract were written from the same mental model, and a test\ncan only fail when they disagree.\n\nThat \"green since commit 1\" fact is the real tell. A suite that has *never* gone red at an\nintegration boundary has never exercised that boundary; it has verified a closed, self-consistent\nsystem.\n\n### The 6-decimals detail made it worse\n\nSetting the mock to 6 decimals modeled the one USDT quirk you already knew about, which is exactly\nwhat makes the mock feel like \"we accounted for USDT.\" A mock is a written-down copy of your\nassumptions about a dependency. It can encode known unknowns. It cannot encode unknown unknowns —\nand the return-value omission was an unknown unknown.\n\n### Why *more* mock tests are structurally incapable, not merely insufficient\n\nThe bug is not on an unreached code path. Every line ran; `forge coverage` was almost certainly\n100%, and that is precisely why it lied — coverage measures **which of your lines executed**, never\n**which counterparty bytecode they executed against**. Concretely:\n\n| Additional testing | Varies | Why it can't find this |\n|---|---|---|\n| More unit tests | your call sequences | the callee's ABI is held constant |\n| Fuzzing `amount` | the input space | wrong axis — the bug is environmental, not input-dependent |\n| Invariant tests | call orderings | same handler, same mock, same compliant `approve` |\n| More assertions | what you check after | the tx reverts before any assertion is reached |\n| 100% branch coverage | which of *your* branches run | says nothing about the counterparty |\n\nThe one variable that matters — the deployed bytecode at `0xdAC1…1ec7` — is held constant *by\nconstruction* the moment you substitute a mock. To surface the bug with a mock you would have to\nwrite `MissingReturnToken` whose `approve` returns nothing, i.e. you would have to already know the\nanswer. **Tests derived from your model of the world can only find bugs that are already in your\nmodel of the world.** That's the boundary a mock-only suite cannot cross, no matter its size.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Fix 1 — the code\n\n```solidity\n// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT\npragma solidity ^0.8.20;\n\nimport {IERC20} from \"@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/IERC20.sol\";\nimport {SafeERC20} from \"@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/utils/SafeERC20.sol\";\n\ncontract Vault {\n    using SafeERC20 for IERC20;\n\n    IERC20 public immutable asset;\n    IPool  public immutable aavePool;\n\n    function deposit(uint256 amount) external returns (uint256 shares) {\n        // 1. measure what actually arrived — do not trust `amount`\n        uint256 balBefore = asset.balanceOf(address(this));\n        asset.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount);\n        uint256 received = asset.balanceOf(address(this)) - balBefore;\n\n        // 2. forceApprove: tolerates a missing return value AND the non-zero -> non-zero guard\n        asset.forceApprove(address(aavePool), received);\n\n        // 3. supply what we actually hold\n        aavePool.supply(address(asset), received, address(this), 0);\n\n        shares = _mintSharesFor(msg.sender, received);   // shares from `received`, not `amount`\n    }\n}\n```\n\n**Why `forceApprove` and not `approve`/`safeApprove`:**\n\n```solidity\n// OpenZeppelin >= 4.9\nfunction forceApprove(IERC20 token, address spender, uint256 value) internal {\n    bytes memory approvalCall = abi.encodeCall(token.approve, (spender, value));\n    if (!_callOptionalReturnBool(token, approvalCall)) {\n        _callOptionalReturn(token, abi.encodeCall(token.approve, (spender, 0)));\n        _callOptionalReturn(token, approvalCall);\n    }\n}\n```\n\nIt fixes both USDT landmines at once: `_callOptionalReturnBool` accepts empty returndata, and the\nzero-then-set fallback survives the anti-race `require`. `safeApprove` (OZ 4.x, deprecated; removed\nin 5.x) is the wrong tool — it *reverts* when the current allowance and the new value are both\nnon-zero. If you're pinned to an OZ version without `forceApprove`, upgrade; the manual equivalent\nis `safeApprove(spender, 0)` followed by `safeApprove(spender, value)`.\n\n**Why the balance-delta:** USDT's `transferFrom` has a built-in fee path\n(`fee = _value * basisPointsRate / 10000`, capped at `maximumFee`). `basisPointsRate` is 0 today, but\nit is owner-settable. If it is ever turned on, `supply(amount)` while holding `amount - fee` reverts\n— or, once the vault has other users' idle balance, silently supplies their funds. Measuring the\ndelta is correct for every token and costs one `SLOAD`-backed `balanceOf`.\n\n**Enforce the call-site rule mechanically** — the fix above is one line; keeping it fixed is the\nhard part:\n\n```bash\n# CI gate: no raw ERC-20 mutators on external tokens.\n# `.safeTransferFrom(` does not match `\\.transferFrom\\(`, so SafeERC20 calls pass.\n! grep -rnE '\\.(approve|transfer|transferFrom)\\(' src/ --include='*.sol'\n```\n\nAllowlist the deliberate exceptions (e.g. your own share token) with a `// solhint-disable-next-line`\nstyle marker rather than loosening the pattern. `slither --detect unchecked-transfer,incorrect-equality`\ncatches the same class.\n\n**Also fix the deploy script and the tests.** A test contract that calls\n`IERC20(USDT).approve(address(vault), amt)` to set up a fork test hits the *identical* decode revert.\nUse `SafeERC20.forceApprove(IERC20(USDT), address(vault), amt)` there too.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Fix 2 — the change in testing practice\n\n### The rule\n\n> **Every address that will be a real deployed contract in production must be exercised as that real\n> deployed contract, on a fork of the target chain, in at least one test on the critical path.**\n>\n> Mocks are for reaching states you *cannot* reach on a fork — pool paused, supply cap hit, oracle\n> stale, `transferFrom` returning `false`. They are not stand-ins for the happy path.\n\nA mock-only suite tests your code against your assumptions. A fork test tests your code against\nreality. You need both, and only the second one can fail for a reason you didn't think of.\n\n### The test that would have caught this\n\n```solidity\n// test/fork/VaultUsdtFork.t.sol\n// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT\npragma solidity ^0.8.20;\n\nimport {Test} from \"forge-std/Test.sol\";\nimport {IERC20} from \"@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/IERC20.sol\";\nimport {SafeERC20} from \"@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/utils/SafeERC20.sol\";\nimport {Vault} from \"../../src/Vault.sol\";\n\ncontract VaultUsdtForkTest is Test {\n    // re-verify against the official Aave address book before trusting these\n    address constant USDT      = 0xdAC17F958D2ee523a2206206994597C13D831ec7;\n    address constant AAVE_POOL = 0x87870Bca3F3fD6335C3F4ce8392D69350B4fA4E2; // Aave V3 mainnet Pool\n    address constant AUSDT     = 0x23878914EFE38d27C4D67Ab83ed1b93A74D4086a; // aEthUSDT\n\n    Vault vault;\n    address alice = makeAddr(\"alice\");\n\n    function setUp() public {\n        vm.createSelectFork(\"mainnet\", 19_000_000);   // pinned => reproducible\n        vault = new Vault(IERC20(USDT), AAVE_POOL);\n        deal(USDT, alice, 1_000_000e6);\n    }\n\n    function test_DepositSuppliesToAave() public {\n        uint256 amount = 10_000e6;\n\n        vm.startPrank(alice);\n        // NOTE: even here you cannot write IERC20(USDT).approve(...) — same decode revert.\n        SafeERC20.forceApprove(IERC20(USDT), address(vault), amount);\n        vault.deposit(amount);\n        vm.stopPrank();\n\n        assertEq(IERC20(USDT).balanceOf(address(vault)), 0, \"no idle USDT left in vault\");\n        assertApproxEqAbs(IERC20(AUSDT).balanceOf(address(vault)), amount, 1, \"aUSDT minted 1:1\");\n        assertGt(vault.balanceOf(alice), 0, \"shares minted\");\n    }\n\n    // second deposit: catches residual-allowance / approve-race regressions\n    function test_ConsecutiveDepositsSucceed() public {\n        _deposit(alice, 5_000e6);\n        _deposit(alice, 5_000e6);\n        assertApproxEqAbs(IERC20(AUSDT).balanceOf(address(vault)), 10_000e6, 2);\n    }\n\n    // property, not implementation mirror: you get back what you put in\n    function testFuzz_DepositWithdrawRoundtrip(uint256 amount) public {\n        amount = bound(amount, 1e6, 500_000e6);\n        uint256 before = IERC20(USDT).balanceOf(alice);\n        _deposit(alice, amount);\n        vm.prank(alice);\n        vault.withdraw(vault.balanceOf(alice));\n        assertGe(IERC20(USDT).balanceOf(alice), before - 1, \"roundtrip loses at most 1 wei\");\n    }\n}\n```\n\nAgainst the current code this fails in `setUp`-adjacent territory on the very first `vault.deposit`,\nwith empty revert data — the exact mainnet failure, reproduced locally, for the cost of one RPC key.\n\n```toml\n# foundry.toml\n[rpc_endpoints]\nmainnet = \"${MAINNET_RPC_URL}\"\n\n[profile.fork]\n# fork tests are slower + need network; separate profile, but REQUIRED on release tags\n```\n\n```bash\nFOUNDRY_PROFILE=fork forge test --match-path 'test/fork/**' -vvv\n```\n\nPin the block so results are reproducible and Foundry's RPC cache makes reruns fast. Make the fork\nprofile a required check on release tags even if you keep it off the per-PR path for RPC flakiness.\n\n### Three supporting changes\n\n**a) An adversarial token matrix, not one friendly mock.** Keep unit tests fast by mocking, but mock\n*hostile* tokens. Make the shared behaviour abstract and re-run it against each:\n\n```solidity\nabstract contract VaultBehaviour is Test {\n    function _newToken() internal virtual returns (address);\n    // ...all shared deposit/withdraw/accounting tests live here...\n}\n\ncontract Vault_StandardToken   is VaultBehaviour { function _newToken() internal override returns (address) { return address(new MockERC20()); } }\ncontract Vault_MissingReturn   is VaultBehaviour { /* approve/transfer return nothing — USDT-shaped   */ }\ncontract Vault_ReturnsFalse    is VaultBehaviour { /* returns false instead of reverting             */ }\ncontract Vault_FeeOnTransfer   is VaultBehaviour { /* recipient gets less than `amount`              */ }\ncontract Vault_Blocklist       is VaultBehaviour { /* reverts for specific addresses — USDC/USDT     */ }\ncontract Vault_RevertOnZero    is VaultBehaviour { /* reverts on a 0-value transfer                  */ }\n```\n\nSteal the implementations from `d-xo/weird-erc20`. This covers the *class* of bug in a fast suite;\nthe fork test covers the *specific instance*. Every new supported asset then inherits coverage for\nfree.\n\n**b) A pre-deploy simulation gate.** Before any mainnet deploy, run the real deploy script plus a\nfirst user transaction against a fork of mainnet **at head**, with the exact constructor args you're\nabout to broadcast:\n\n```bash\nforge script script/Deploy.s.sol --rpc-url $MAINNET_RPC --sig 'run()' -vvvv   # no --broadcast\n```\n\nExtend the script with a post-deploy smoke `deposit()`. This alone would have caught it in under a\nminute. The root process failure was deploying a `(vault, token, pool)` triple that had never been\nexecuted together anywhere.\n\n**c) Treat \"green since the first commit\" as a defect signal.** Add one negative control: break the\nintegration on purpose (delete the `approve`, point the pool at `address(0)`, return `false` from the\nmock's `transfer`) and confirm the suite goes red. If it doesn't, those tests aren't testing what\ntheir names claim. Formalize it with mutation testing on the integration layer if you want it\ncontinuous.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Pre-deploy checklist delta\n\n- [ ] No raw `.approve` / `.transfer` / `.transferFrom` on external tokens — CI grep gate\n- [ ] `forceApprove`, never `approve` / `safeApprove`\n- [ ] Amounts derived from measured balance deltas, not from arguments\n- [ ] Fork test on the critical path for **every** production (token, protocol, chain) triple\n- [ ] Fork tests: pinned block, in CI, required for release\n- [ ] Unit suite parameterized over the weird-ERC20 matrix\n- [ ] Deploy script simulated against mainnet-at-head with production args before broadcast\n- [ ] At least one deliberate break proves the integration tests can fail\n\n---\n\n## Open questions\n\n1. Which OZ version are you on? `forceApprove` needs ≥4.9; on 5.x `safeApprove` is gone entirely.\n2. Does the vault already hold idle balance (fees, donations, other users)? If so the balance-delta\n   pattern needs a reentrancy guard on `deposit` so two in-flight deposits can't misattribute the\n   delta.\n3. Is the deployed vault upgradeable, or does fixing this mean a redeploy plus migration? If funds\n   are stuck, that changes the priority order of everything above.\n4. Which other assets are planned? USDC adds a blocklist and an upgradeable proxy; stETH adds\n   rebasing (the balance-delta pattern is necessary but not sufficient there).\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":857,"cache_read_input_tokens":30507,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":0,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":857},"output_tokens":3,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"not_available"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"05c6e27b-2c33-45a9-a422-91623bbf885f","uuid":"edbe551f-0c24-4454-8550-eac23f0b2fd7","timestamp":"2026-07-27T08:11:41.780Z","request_id":"req_011CdSDmMsm4Z2iWNuJLqc8P"}

Why it reverts against the real deployed USDT\n\nTether's `TetherToken` (0xdAC1…1ec7, Solidity 0.4.17) predates the finalized ERC-20 ABI. Its\nmutating functions are declared with **no return value**:\n\n```solidity\n// as deployed on mainnet\nfunction transfer(address _to, uint _value) public onlyPayloadSize(2 * 32);\nfunction transferFrom(address _from, address _to, uint _value) public onlyPayloadSize(3 * 32);\nfunction approve(address _spender, uint _value) public onlyPayloadSize(2 * 32);\n```\n\nYour contract calls it through OpenZeppelin's `IERC20`, which declares `approve` as\n`returns (bool)`. For any external call with a declared return type, Solidity ≥0.8 emits roughly:\n\n```\nsuccess := call(gas(), token, 0, in, insize, 0, 0)\nif iszero(success) { returndatacopy(0, 0, returndatasize()) revert(0, returndatasize()) }\nif iszero(gt(returndatasize(), 31)) { revert(0, 0) }      // <-- fires here\nreturndatacopy(...)                                        // decode the bool\n```\n\nSequence of events on mainnet:\n\n1. The `CALL` to USDT **succeeds**. The allowance is actually written inside USDT's frame.\n2. USDT's function ends with no `RETURN` payload → `returndatasize() == 0`.\n3. Your frame hits the ABI-decoder length check, `revert(0, 0)`, and the whole transaction —\n   including the allowance write and the earlier `safeTransferFrom` — is rolled back.\n\n`revert(0, 0)` produces **zero bytes of revert data**: no `Error(string)`, no custom error selector,\nno `Panic(uint256)` code. That is exactly the \"revert carries no reason string\" you observed.\n\n### The empty revert data is itself the diagnostic\n\nIt rules out the other two lines:\n\n- **Line 1 (`safeTransferFrom`)** would revert with `SafeERC20FailedOperation(address)` (OZ 5.x) or\n  `\"SafeERC20: low-level call failed\"` (OZ 4.x) — never empty. It didn't revert anyway.\n- **Line 3 (`aavePool.supply`)** — Aave V3's `IPool.supply` is declared with no return value, so it\n  has no decode step to fail. Its own failures (`RESERVE_FROZEN`, `SUPPLY_CAP_EXCEEDED`,\n  `INVALID_AMOUNT`) surface as `Errors.*` reason strings like `\"28\"`. Also never empty.\n\nEmpty returndata on a call to a pre-ABI token is a fingerprint. Confirm it in one command:\n\n```bash\n# declared WITH a bool return -> cast fails to decode\ncast call 0xdAC17F958D2ee523a2206206994597C13D831ec7 \\\n  \"approve(address,uint256)(bool)\" 0x87870Bca3F3fD6335C3F4ce8392D69350B4fA4E2 1000000 \\\n  --from <any-holder> --rpc-url $MAINNET_RPC\n\n# declared WITHOUT a return -> succeeds, prints \"0x\" (returndatasize == 0)\ncast call 0xdAC17F958D2ee523a2206206994597C13D831ec7 \\\n  \"approve(address,uint256)\" 0x87870Bca3F3fD6335C3F4ce8392D69350B4fA4E2 1000000 \\\n  --from <any-holder> --rpc-url $MAINNET_RPC\n\ncast interface 0xdAC17F958D2ee523a2206206994597C13D831ec7   # shows the real, return-less ABI\n```\n\n### The second landmine on the same line\n\nUSDT's `approve` also carries the anti-race guard:\n\n```solidity\nrequire(!((_value != 0) && (allowed[msg.sender][_spender] != 0)));\n```\n\nYou cannot move a **non-zero** allowance directly to another **non-zero** value; you must zero it\nfirst. In *this exact* sequence it's dormant — `Pool.supply` pulls the full `amount`, so the\nallowance returns to 0 before the next deposit. It goes live the moment approved ≠ pulled: an\ninfinite approval, a partial fill, dust left by a fee-on-transfer token, or a future integration that\napproves and then takes a different branch. Being 0.4.17, that `require` has no message either — so\nwhen it does fire, it also reverts with **no reason string**. Worth closing now, for free, with the\nsame fix.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Why `using SafeERC20 for IERC20` did not protect the failing line\n\n`using L for T` **attaches** library functions as members of `T`. It never **replaces** an existing\nmember of `T`, and it cannot rename anything.\n\n- `IERC20` already has a member called `approve`. `usdt.approve(...)` resolves to that interface\n  function — a plain, unwrapped external call. There is no ambiguity for the compiler to flag.\n- SafeERC20 does not define a function named `approve` at all. It defines `safeTransfer`,\n  `safeTransferFrom`, `forceApprove`, `safeIncreaseAllowance`, `safeDecreaseAllowance` (and, in OZ\n  4.x, the deprecated `safeApprove`). Different names ⇒ nothing to shadow.\n\nSo line 1 opted in by typing `safeTransferFrom`; line 2 opted out by typing `approve`. SafeERC20's\nprotection is in `_callOptionalReturn`, which tolerates a missing return value:\n\n```solidity\n// OpenZeppelin 5.x\nfunction _callOptionalReturn(IERC20 token, bytes memory data) private {\n    bytes memory returndata = address(token).functionCall(data);\n    if (returndata.length != 0 && !abi.decode(returndata, (bool))) {\n        revert SafeERC20FailedOperation(address(token));\n    }\n}\n```\n\n`returndata.length != 0 &&` is the entire fix: zero-length returndata is treated as success, and the\naddress-has-code check lives in `functionCall`. Line 2 never reached this code.\n\n**Generalize it:** `using SafeERC20 for IERC20` is not a safety property of the contract. It is\nautocomplete. The only thing that makes a token call safe is the *name you typed at the call site*.\nA single `.approve(`, `.transfer(`, or `.transferFrom(` anywhere in the codebase is unprotected,\nand the compiler will never say so. This is why the rule has to be mechanically enforced (§4).\n\n---\n\n## 3. Why the mock could never fail, and why more mock tests would not have helped\n\n### The mock cannot disagree with you\n\n`MockERC20` is a stock OZ `ERC20`. Its `approve` ends with `return true` — 32 bytes, `0x…01`. The\ndecoder check `returndatasize() > 31` passes. There is no input, no ordering, no amount, no caller,\nand no state that makes a compliant token return zero bytes. **The failure mode does not exist in\nthe mock's state space.** The suite has been green since the first commit not because the code is\ncorrect but because the mock and the contract were written from the same mental model, and a test\ncan only fail when they disagree.\n\nThat \"green since commit 1\" fact is the real tell. A suite that has *never* gone red at an\nintegration boundary has never exercised that boundary; it has verified a closed, self-consistent\nsystem.\n\n### The 6-decimals detail made it worse\n\nSetting the mock to 6 decimals modeled the one USDT quirk you already knew about, which is exactly\nwhat makes the mock feel like \"we accounted for USDT.\" A mock is a written-down copy of your\nassumptions about a dependency. It can encode known unknowns. It cannot encode unknown unknowns —\nand the return-value omission was an unknown unknown.\n\n### Why *more* mock tests are structurally incapable, not merely insufficient\n\nThe bug is not on an unreached code path. Every line ran; `forge coverage` was almost certainly\n100%, and that is precisely why it lied — coverage measures **which of your lines executed**, never\n**which counterparty bytecode they executed against**. Concretely:\n\n| Additional testing | Varies | Why it can't find this |\n|---|---|---|\n| More unit tests | your call sequences | the callee's ABI is held constant |\n| Fuzzing `amount` | the input space | wrong axis — the bug is environmental, not input-dependent |\n| Invariant tests | call orderings | same handler, same mock, same compliant `approve` |\n| More assertions | what you check after | the tx reverts before any assertion is reached |\n| 100% branch coverage | which of *your* branches run | says nothing about the counterparty |\n\nThe one variable that matters — the deployed bytecode at `0xdAC1…1ec7` — is held constant *by\nconstruction* the moment you substitute a mock. To surface the bug with a mock you would have to\nwrite `MissingReturnToken` whose `approve` returns nothing, i.e. you would have to already know the\nanswer. **Tests derived from your model of the world can only find bugs that are already in your\nmodel of the world.** That's the boundary a mock-only suite cannot cross, no matter its size.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Fix 1 — the code\n\n```solidity\n// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT\npragma solidity ^0.8.20;\n\nimport {IERC20} from \"@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/IERC20.sol\";\nimport {SafeERC20} from \"@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/utils/SafeERC20.sol\";\n\ncontract Vault {\n    using SafeERC20 for IERC20;\n\n    IERC20 public immutable asset;\n    IPool  public immutable aavePool;\n\n    function deposit(uint256 amount) external returns (uint256 shares) {\n        // 1. measure what actually arrived — do not trust `amount`\n        uint256 balBefore = asset.balanceOf(address(this));\n        asset.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount);\n        uint256 received = asset.balanceOf(address(this)) - balBefore;\n\n        // 2. forceApprove: tolerates a missing return value AND the non-zero -> non-zero guard\n        asset.forceApprove(address(aavePool), received);\n\n        // 3. supply what we actually hold\n        aavePool.supply(address(asset), received, address(this), 0);\n\n        shares = _mintSharesFor(msg.sender, received);   // shares from `received`, not `amount`\n    }\n}\n```\n\n**Why `forceApprove` and not `approve`/`safeApprove`:**\n\n```solidity\n// OpenZeppelin >= 4.9\nfunction forceApprove(IERC20 token, address spender, uint256 value) internal {\n    bytes memory approvalCall = abi.encodeCall(token.approve, (spender, value));\n    if (!_callOptionalReturnBool(token, approvalCall)) {\n        _callOptionalReturn(token, abi.encodeCall(token.approve, (spender, 0)));\n        _callOptionalReturn(token, approvalCall);\n    }\n}\n```\n\nIt fixes both USDT landmines at once: `_callOptionalReturnBool` accepts empty returndata, and the\nzero-then-set fallback survives the anti-race `require`. `safeApprove` (OZ 4.x, deprecated; removed\nin 5.x) is the wrong tool — it *reverts* when the current allowance and the new value are both\nnon-zero. If you're pinned to an OZ version without `forceApprove`, upgrade; the manual equivalent\nis `safeApprove(spender, 0)` followed by `safeApprove(spender, value)`.\n\n**Why the balance-delta:** USDT's `transferFrom` has a built-in fee path\n(`fee = _value * basisPointsRate / 10000`, capped at `maximumFee`). `basisPointsRate` is 0 today, but\nit is owner-settable. If it is ever turned on, `supply(amount)` while holding `amount - fee` reverts\n— or, once the vault has other users' idle balance, silently supplies their funds. Measuring the\ndelta is correct for every token and costs one `SLOAD`-backed `balanceOf`.\n\n**Enforce the call-site rule mechanically** — the fix above is one line; keeping it fixed is the\nhard part:\n\n```bash\n# CI gate: no raw ERC-20 mutators on external tokens.\n# `.safeTransferFrom(` does not match `\\.transferFrom\\(`, so SafeERC20 calls pass.\n! grep -rnE '\\.(approve|transfer|transferFrom)\\(' src/ --include='*.sol'\n```\n\nAllowlist the deliberate exceptions (e.g. your own share token) with a `// solhint-disable-next-line`\nstyle marker rather than loosening the pattern. `slither --detect unchecked-transfer,incorrect-equality`\ncatches the same class.\n\n**Also fix the deploy script and the tests.** A test contract that calls\n`IERC20(USDT).approve(address(vault), amt)` to set up a fork test hits the *identical* decode revert.\nUse `SafeERC20.forceApprove(IERC20(USDT), address(vault), amt)` there too.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Fix 2 — the change in testing practice\n\n### The rule\n\n> **Every address that will be a real deployed contract in production must be exercised as that real\n> deployed contract, on a fork of the target chain, in at least one test on the critical path.**\n>\n> Mocks are for reaching states you *cannot* reach on a fork — pool paused, supply cap hit, oracle\n> stale, `transferFrom` returning `false`. They are not stand-ins for the happy path.\n\nA mock-only suite tests your code against your assumptions. A fork test tests your code against\nreality. You need both, and only the second one can fail for a reason you didn't think of.\n\n### The test that would have caught this\n\n```solidity\n// test/fork/VaultUsdtFork.t.sol\n// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT\npragma solidity ^0.8.20;\n\nimport {Test} from \"forge-std/Test.sol\";\nimport {IERC20} from \"@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/IERC20.sol\";\nimport {SafeERC20} from \"@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/utils/SafeERC20.sol\";\nimport {Vault} from \"../../src/Vault.sol\";\n\ncontract VaultUsdtForkTest is Test {\n    // re-verify against the official Aave address book before trusting these\n    address constant USDT      = 0xdAC17F958D2ee523a2206206994597C13D831ec7;\n    address constant AAVE_POOL = 0x87870Bca3F3fD6335C3F4ce8392D69350B4fA4E2; // Aave V3 mainnet Pool\n    address constant AUSDT     = 0x23878914EFE38d27C4D67Ab83ed1b93A74D4086a; // aEthUSDT\n\n    Vault vault;\n    address alice = makeAddr(\"alice\");\n\n    function setUp() public {\n        vm.createSelectFork(\"mainnet\", 19_000_000);   // pinned => reproducible\n        vault = new Vault(IERC20(USDT), AAVE_POOL);\n        deal(USDT, alice, 1_000_000e6);\n    }\n\n    function test_DepositSuppliesToAave() public {\n        uint256 amount = 10_000e6;\n\n        vm.startPrank(alice);\n        // NOTE: even here you cannot write IERC20(USDT).approve(...) — same decode revert.\n        SafeERC20.forceApprove(IERC20(USDT), address(vault), amount);\n        vault.deposit(amount);\n        vm.stopPrank();\n\n        assertEq(IERC20(USDT).balanceOf(address(vault)), 0, \"no idle USDT left in vault\");\n        assertApproxEqAbs(IERC20(AUSDT).balanceOf(address(vault)), amount, 1, \"aUSDT minted 1:1\");\n        assertGt(vault.balanceOf(alice), 0, \"shares minted\");\n    }\n\n    // second deposit: catches residual-allowance / approve-race regressions\n    function test_ConsecutiveDepositsSucceed() public {\n        _deposit(alice, 5_000e6);\n        _deposit(alice, 5_000e6);\n        assertApproxEqAbs(IERC20(AUSDT).balanceOf(address(vault)), 10_000e6, 2);\n    }\n\n    // property, not implementation mirror: you get back what you put in\n    function testFuzz_DepositWithdrawRoundtrip(uint256 amount) public {\n        amount = bound(amount, 1e6, 500_000e6);\n        uint256 before = IERC20(USDT).balanceOf(alice);\n        _deposit(alice, amount);\n        vm.prank(alice);\n        vault.withdraw(vault.balanceOf(alice));\n        assertGe(IERC20(USDT).balanceOf(alice), before - 1, \"roundtrip loses at most 1 wei\");\n    }\n}\n```\n\nAgainst the current code this fails in `setUp`-adjacent territory on the very first `vault.deposit`,\nwith empty revert data — the exact mainnet failure, reproduced locally, for the cost of one RPC key.\n\n```toml\n# foundry.toml\n[rpc_endpoints]\nmainnet = \"${MAINNET_RPC_URL}\"\n\n[profile.fork]\n# fork tests are slower + need network; separate profile, but REQUIRED on release tags\n```\n\n```bash\nFOUNDRY_PROFILE=fork forge test --match-path 'test/fork/**' -vvv\n```\n\nPin the block so results are reproducible and Foundry's RPC cache makes reruns fast. Make the fork\nprofile a required check on release tags even if you keep it off the per-PR path for RPC flakiness.\n\n### Three supporting changes\n\n**a) An adversarial token matrix, not one friendly mock.** Keep unit tests fast by mocking, but mock\n*hostile* tokens. Make the shared behaviour abstract and re-run it against each:\n\n```solidity\nabstract contract VaultBehaviour is Test {\n    function _newToken() internal virtual returns (address);\n    // ...all shared deposit/withdraw/accounting tests live here...\n}\n\ncontract Vault_StandardToken   is VaultBehaviour { function _newToken() internal override returns (address) { return address(new MockERC20()); } }\ncontract Vault_MissingReturn   is VaultBehaviour { /* approve/transfer return nothing — USDT-shaped   */ }\ncontract Vault_ReturnsFalse    is VaultBehaviour { /* returns false instead of reverting             */ }\ncontract Vault_FeeOnTransfer   is VaultBehaviour { /* recipient gets less than `amount`              */ }\ncontract Vault_Blocklist       is VaultBehaviour { /* reverts for specific addresses — USDC/USDT     */ }\ncontract Vault_RevertOnZero    is VaultBehaviour { /* reverts on a 0-value transfer                  */ }\n```\n\nSteal the implementations from `d-xo/weird-erc20`. This covers the *class* of bug in a fast suite;\nthe fork test covers the *specific instance*. Every new supported asset then inherits coverage for\nfree.\n\n**b) A pre-deploy simulation gate.** Before any mainnet deploy, run the real deploy script plus a\nfirst user transaction against a fork of mainnet **at head**, with the exact constructor args you're\nabout to broadcast:\n\n```bash\nforge script script/Deploy.s.sol --rpc-url $MAINNET_RPC --sig 'run()' -vvvv   # no --broadcast\n```\n\nExtend the script with a post-deploy smoke `deposit()`. This alone would have caught it in under a\nminute. The root process failure was deploying a `(vault, token, pool)` triple that had never been\nexecuted together anywhere.\n\n**c) Treat \"green since the first commit\" as a defect signal.** Add one negative control: break the\nintegration on purpose (delete the `approve`, point the pool at `address(0)`, return `false` from the\nmock's `transfer`) and confirm the suite goes red. If it doesn't, those tests aren't testing what\ntheir names claim. Formalize it with mutation testing on the integration layer if you want it\ncontinuous.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Pre-deploy checklist delta\n\n- [ ] No raw `.approve` / `.transfer` / `.transferFrom` on external tokens — CI grep gate\n- [ ] `forceApprove`, never `approve` / `safeApprove`\n- [ ] Amounts derived from measured balance deltas, not from arguments\n- [ ] Fork test on the critical path for **every** production (token, protocol, chain) triple\n- [ ] Fork tests: pinned block, in CI, required for release\n- [ ] Unit suite parameterized over the weird-ERC20 matrix\n- [ ] Deploy script simulated against mainnet-at-head with production args before broadcast\n- [ ] At least one deliberate break proves the integration tests can fail\n\n---\n\n## Open questions\n\n1. Which OZ version are you on? `forceApprove` needs ≥4.9; on 5.x `safeApprove` is gone entirely.\n2. Does the vault already hold idle balance (fees, donations, other users)? If so the balance-delta\n   pattern needs a reentrancy guard on `deposit` so two in-flight deposits can't misattribute the\n   delta.\n3. Is the deployed vault upgradeable, or does fixing this mean a redeploy plus migration? If funds\n   are stuck, that changes the priority order of everything above.\n4. Which other assets are planned? USDC adds a blocklist and an upgradeable proxy; stETH adds\n   rebasing (the balance-delta pattern is necessary but not sufficient there).\n","structuredPatch":[],"originalFile":null,"userModified":false}}
